title: Write Prologue (After Chapter Outline Exists)
steps: Write the Prologue for "The Signal Beneath"

response.assistant_message: Queuing the prologue for "The Signal Beneath" — I'll let you know when it's ready.

result.content_text:
The sun went down behind the tree line at 7:43, and Mara was already at her bench.

She knew the time without looking. The light changed in a particular way when it dropped below the oaks, a slow bronze draining out of the workshop's west window, leaving the room the color of old newsprint, and she had watched it happen often enough that her body had learned to read it. She set down the watch she'd been cleaning, a Seiko with a cracked crystal and a mainspring she'd coaxed back to tension with a piece of shim stock, and pulled the logbook toward her.

Entry 2,547.

She wrote the number in the top right corner of the page, then the date, then the time to the minute. She wrote with a carpenter's pencil because the graphite didn't freeze in winter and didn't bleed when the roof leaked, and the logbook itself was a hardcover ledger she'd found sealed in a Ziploc bag in the back of a dead accountant's filing cabinet three years ago. Forty pages left. She tried not to think about that.

The receiver sat on the bench to her left, a Grundig Satellit 750, which had been a beautiful machine once, the kind of radio that serious hobbyists kept in padded cases and talked about on forums that no longer existed. She'd found it in the third winter, in a house four blocks over, under a collapsed section of ceiling that had protected it from the rain. The cabinet had a long crack along the top and the LCD display was dead, but the analog dial still worked and the circuitry had survived. She'd spent two weeks cleaning the contacts, replacing three capacitors with salvaged equivalents, and rigging a regulated power supply from a pair of lead-acid batteries she kept on a trickle charge from a small solar panel bolted to the south-facing slope of the barn roof. The audio was narrow and hissy, the tuning knob scratched like gravel in a tin can, and the S-meter needle had a tremor in the lower half of its range that she'd never been able to fix. She loved it the way you love a difficult thing you have kept alive.

She switched it on. The hiss came up slowly as the set warmed, a broad white noise that filled the workshop and pressed against the walls, and she let it run while she uncapped her pencil and wrote the first entry of the night.

*1945h. 7.200 MHz. Band condition: poor. Noise floor elevated, solar activity probable. No carriers. Silence.*

She moved the dial. The knob resisted slightly at first, the way it always did until the mechanism warmed, and then it turned with a slow, grinding smoothness she found satisfying. She worked through the forty-meter band in methodical steps, pausing at each frequency long enough to let the ionosphere give her something if it had anything to give. It rarely did. The high-frequency spectrum had been a crowded place once, religious broadcasters, number stations, ham operators, utility traffic, the BBC World Service in six languages, and now it was mostly this: hiss, and the occasional pop of atmospheric discharge, and the warbling heterodyne tone of two dead carriers beating against each other somewhere in the middle distance.

The workshop smelled of solder and machine oil and the faint sourness of the dried beans she kept in sealed tins along the north wall, stacked eight high between the tool rack and the door. The beans were this year's trade surplus, she'd repaired a hand-cranked water pump for the Keller settlement in March and they'd paid her in legumes, which was a fair price and she hadn't argued. She had four months of food if she was careful, six if the kitchen garden held. She was always careful.

She noted two more entries. Both silence.

Outside, the suburb made its nighttime sounds. Wind moved through the gutters of the house next door, the one with the collapsed garage, whose owner she had never known, whose driveway she walked past every time she went to the road. Somewhere in the tangle of what had been a cul-de-sac, a piece of loose aluminum siding ticked against a fascia board in the breeze, a small regular sound like a clock with a damaged escapement. She had stopped noticing these sounds years ago. They were the texture of silence now, the way silence actually sounded when everything else was gone.

*1958h. 9.555 MHz. Band condition: poor-to-fair. Possible carrier, very weak, drifting. Unresolved. Silence.*

She held the dial still and listened to the possible carrier for a full minute. It was the kind of thing that could be a signal or could be the receiver's own oscillator doing something strange when the temperature changed, the Grundig had a calibration drift she'd mapped carefully over three winters, a tendency to wander sharp by about two kilohertz when the workshop dropped below forty degrees. It was sixty degrees tonight, maybe a little less. She marked the entry with a question mark and moved on.

Entry 2,547. The number sat in the corner of the page and looked back at her.

She had started the logbook on the forty-second day after the Cascade, when she had understood that the silence was not temporary. Before that she had been doing what everyone was doing: moving, looking for food, looking for people, not sleeping enough, not thinking clearly. The logbook was the thing that had stopped her from unraveling. She had written the first entry in a spiral notebook with a ballpoint pen that had run dry on page nine, and she had kept going in pencil, and then in a second notebook, and then a third, and now this ledger with forty pages left. Every night she had done this. Every night she had heard nothing worth hearing.

She was not waiting for anything. She had stopped waiting years ago. This was just what she did at night, the same way she wound the watches on her bench every morning and checked the battery voltage on the solar array every afternoon and walked the perimeter of the property every evening before dark. It was maintenance. It was the discipline of keeping a thing functioning against the pressure of entropy, which was the only pressure the world exerted now.

She moved through the twenty-five-meter band. Silence. The thirty-one-meter band. Silence, and then a faint burst of what might have been voice, she held the dial, leaned toward the speaker, and then it was gone, swallowed by a rising wall of atmospheric noise that lifted the hiss two full notches and buried everything underneath it.

She wrote: *2011h. 9.745 MHz. Voice burst, one second, unintelligible. Noise floor rising. Band closing.*

She noted the time the band closed. She noted the temperature inside the workshop. She noted the battery voltage, which had sagged slightly under the receiver's load, the way it always did in the evening when the solar panel had stopped contributing and she was drawing down the reserve. She would need to watch that through the winter. She was always watching something through the winter.

The bronze light was gone from the window now. The workshop held only the glow of the single oil lamp she kept on the corner of the bench, a squat glass thing with a wick trimmed to stop it from smoking, burning rendered fat that smelled faintly animal in a way she had long since stopped noticing. In its light the logbook's pages were the color of cream, the pencil lines dark and precise, two thousand five hundred and forty-seven entries of nothing.

She turned to the nineteen-meter band and listened to the world not speaking.

The knock came at seven in the morning, three raps on the gate post, Coll's knock, the one she'd told him to use when he came for equipment.

She was already in the yard, filling the water barrels from the roof-collection tank before the day heated up. She set down the bucket and wiped her hands on her work pants and went to the gate.

Coll was on the other side of the chain-link, a big man gone lean in the years since the Cascade, with a two-wheeled cart he'd built from a bicycle frame and salvaged steel pipe. He had a dog with him, a brindle thing that sat at his heel and watched her with yellow eyes.

"Generator ready?" he said.

"Yesterday." She worked the padlock. "Come in."

He left the cart outside and followed her to the workshop. The dog stayed at the gate without being told.

He picked up the generator from the bench where she'd left it, a hand-crank unit, pre-Cascade, with a cracked housing she'd patched with epoxy and a set of brushes she'd fabricated from copper strip salvaged from a dead transformer. She'd spent four hours on those brushes. He turned it over in his hands the way people turned things over when they didn't know what they were looking at.

"It'll hold," she said. "The brushes are the weak point. Don't let anyone run it for more than twenty minutes without a rest. Ten if they're cranking hard."

"How long?"

"Before the brushes go? Hard to say. Six months if they're careful. Less if they're not."

He nodded and set it back on the bench. Then he unslung the pack from his back and put it on the workbench beside the generator. Two tins of rendered fat, a cloth bag of dried corn, a smaller bag of salt, and a coil of copper wire she hadn't asked for.

"Wire's extra," he said. "Preet at the Keller settlement said to add it. Said you'd know what it was for."

She didn't know what it was for, but copper wire was copper wire. "Tell her I said thank you."

She counted the tins and the salt and moved them to the shelf. Coll watched her work with the patience of a man used to waiting in doorways.

"Heard anything?" he said.

It was the question everyone asked her. She'd learned not to take it personally, they didn't mean anything by it. They just knew she had a receiver.

"Nothing useful."

"RA was on the Whitmore road three days ago." He said it the way people said weather now, not alarmed, just factual, the way you'd note a storm coming. "Four trucks. Headed north."

She stopped moving the tins. "Whitmore's east of here."

"Twenty miles."

That was closer than they'd been since spring. She thought about the antenna wire she had strung along the roofline, visible from the road if you knew what you were looking at. She hadn't worried about it before. She filed the thought away.

"What were they doing on the Whitmore road?"

"Moving through. Preet's nephew saw them, said they weren't stopping, just moving. But they had the white trucks."

The white trucks meant Reclamation Authority enforcement, not just the information teams. The information teams drove gray. She had learned this distinction two years ago from a woman who had made the mistake of not knowing it.

"Harrowfield?" she said.

Coll's expression shifted, not much, just a tightening around the eyes. "Harrowfield's down to maybe sixty people. Half of what it was in the spring."

"Where did they go?"

"Some went to Keller. Some just, " He made a small gesture with one hand. Gone. Into the roads, the fields, the spaces between settlements where people went when they'd run out of places to be. "Millhaven's still standing. Heard they're up to two hundred now. Don't know how."

She'd heard the name Millhaven before, from other traders. A settlement four days west, beyond the Harrow country, in what had been a mid-sized manufacturing town before the Cascade. She had never been there. She had never been anywhere in three years.

"Two hundred is a lot," she said.

"Is now." He picked up the generator. "You need anything? I'm going through Keller day after tomorrow."

She thought about it. "Solder. If anyone has it."

"I'll ask." He tucked the generator under one arm. At the door he paused. "You should think about Millhaven."

She looked at him.

"I'm not telling you your business," he said. "I'm just saying. The eastern roads are getting worse. RA's been through Harrowfield twice this year. Settlements that size don't shrink that fast unless something's pushing them." He shifted the generator. "You're useful out here. But useful doesn't keep you safe."

She held the door open for him and didn't answer.

He walked back to his cart and strapped the generator to the frame with a length of rope he'd looped through the pipe rails. The brindle dog stood and shook itself and fell in beside him without a word from Coll. She watched them go up the cracked road between the weed-choked driveways, the cart wheels finding the smoothest line through the frost-heaved asphalt, until the street curved and he was gone.

She stood at the gate for a moment.

Four trucks on the Whitmore road. Twenty miles.

She went back inside and wrote it in the logbook, not in the signal entries, but in the margin, where she kept the other kind of record. The kind that wasn't about frequencies.

The lamp was a pre-Cascade oil burner she'd converted to run on rendered fat, and it threw a yellow circle across the workbench that was just wide enough to work in. Outside that circle, the workshop went dark fast. She preferred it that way.

The watch had come in with Coll's last run, three weeks back, a pocket watch, brass-cased, with a cracked crystal and a mainspring that had been wound past its limit by someone who didn't know better. The owner wanted it running again. He'd offered two days of labor for it, which was more than the watch was worth, which meant it had been his father's or his son's. She hadn't asked.

She set it under the lamp and picked up the case opener, a thin steel lever she'd ground down from a butter knife, and pressed it into the back seam. The case gave with a soft click. Inside, the movement was a small, dense country of gears and levers, every component interdependent, every tooth in conversation with the next. She had repaired maybe sixty watches since the Cascade. She still felt the same thing when she opened one: a loosening somewhere behind the sternum.

The mainspring was the problem. She could see where it had been stressed, a faint ripple in the metal near the outer coil, a place where it had been pushed past its elastic limit and had not fully returned. She would need to replace it. She had a donor movement in the tin on the second shelf, a cheap quartz watch she'd gutted for parts, and she thought the mainspring might be close enough in width to work.

She got up to check and the fat lamp guttered in the draft from the door seam. She cupped it with her hand until it steadied.

The donor spring was slightly narrower than she wanted but the arbor fit. She carried both movements back to the lamp and began the work of transfer, removing the old spring with the click spring lever, coiling the new one into the barrel with the winding tool, feeling for the point where tension became right rather than tight. It was not a skill she could explain to anyone. It lived in her fingers.

She was fitting the barrel back into the plate when she heard Dani's voice.

Not heard, remembered. But the memory had a physical quality, like a sound carried on the wrong band, arriving from somewhere it shouldn't be able to reach.

*When are you coming back?*

She set down the winding tool.

The voice had come through a Baofeng UV-5R, a cheap handheld she'd given him before she left for the salvage run. She'd programmed both units to the same frequency, 146.520, the old calling channel, the one ham operators had used for simplex contact since before she was born. She'd told him to check in at noon and six. She'd told him the batteries would last four days if he was careful.

*When are you coming back?*

She had been in the basement of a strip mall electronics store forty miles east, in what had been a suburb called Crestfield, working by flashlight through a bin of salvaged components. She'd been looking for a replacement oscillator crystal for the shortwave receiver, a specific cut, 11.0592 MHz, the kind that had been common before the Cascade and was now functionally extinct. She'd found three that were close. She'd been trying to determine if close was close enough.

She'd keyed the radio and told him two more days.

He'd said *okay* in the way he always said okay, which was not quite agreement and not quite protest, just an acknowledgment that she had spoken and he had heard and he would wait because there was nothing else to do. He'd been twenty-two. He'd had a way of making a single word carry the weight of a longer sentence.

She'd found the crystal on the second day. It wasn't the right cut, 11.0592 it was not, but 10.000 MHz, close enough to retune around, close enough to make the receiver work if she adjusted the front-end filter. She'd packed it in cotton wool inside a mint tin and started back.

She'd been six hours out when the fever hit the settlement.

Not a fast fever. A slow one, the kind that starts as a sore throat and a tiredness that seems like ordinary tiredness. By the time it was recognizable as something worse, it had been in the settlement for three days. By the time she got back, Dani had been sick for two of them.

He'd died on a Tuesday. She knew it was Tuesday because she'd been keeping a log even then, even in the first terrible year, because it was the only way she knew how to hold onto time. She had written: *0900 local. D. gone. Fever. No antibiotics. Nothing I could have done.* She had written that last sentence and then crossed it out and written it again and crossed it out again and left the page with two crossed-out lines and nothing else.

She picked up the winding tool.

The mainspring seated correctly on the third try. She fitted the barrel cap and tested the click, the small ratchet that prevented the spring from unwinding during winding, the part that kept all the stored tension from releasing at once. It held. She began reassembling the movement plate by plate, each screw torqued to feel rather than specification, each jewel checked for seating before she moved to the next layer.

The oscillator crystal was still in the receiver. Had been for seven years. The receiver worked because of it, not perfectly, the calibration drifted half a kilohertz warm and she'd learned to compensate, but it worked. She had never decided how to feel about that.

She set the hands to midnight, which was where she always set them when she had no other information, and wound the crown eight turns and listened to the tick. It was slightly fast, she could hear it, a tick that came a fraction too soon, a movement running a little hot. She turned the regulator lever a hair toward the minus sign and wound it again and listened.

Better. Not perfect. Close enough.

She set the watch on the bench beside the lamp and wrote in the repair log: *Pocket watch, brass, open-face. Mainspring replaced, donor movement, 10.5mm wide, slight undersize, functional. Regulator adjusted -0.3mm. Running slightly fast; advise owner to set against solar noon and check weekly.* She noted the date and the owner's name and closed the log.

The lamp had burned down a third of an inch while she worked. Outside, the wind had picked up, she could hear it moving through the loose aluminum siding on the garage, a sound like something trying to get in without quite committing to it.

She looked at the watch.

It ticked with the small, certain sound of a thing that had been broken and was now, within its limits, whole. She had made that happen. She was good at making that happen.

She was less good at the other things.

She turned off the lamp and sat in the dark for a moment, listening to the wind and the tick and the silence beneath both of them, the deep suburban silence that had no traffic in it, no HVAC hum, no neighbor's television bleeding through the wall, just the dark and the cold and the small machine on the bench, counting out the seconds with perfect indifference.

Then she got up and went to the receiver.

The radio room had been a pantry. She had chosen it for the same reason she'd chosen the basement workshop, no windows, one door, easy to seal, and she had spent three days in the first year stripping the shelves and running the antenna cable through a hole she'd drilled in the ceiling and sealed with plumber's putty that had since hardened to the color of old bone. The putty had cracked along one edge last winter. She'd repacked it with candle wax and electrical tape and it had held, more or less, which was the standard she applied to most things now.

The receiver sat on a folding table she'd dragged from a neighbor's garage, the table's legs shimmed level with folded cardboard because the floor had settled unevenly sometime in the third or fourth year. The set itself was a Grundig Satellit 750 that had survived the Cascade in a Faraday-adjacent accident, stored inside a steel filing cabinet in a concrete-floored storage unit, surrounded by enough metal to blunt the induced current. She'd found it fourteen months after the Cascade, traded a rebuilt bicycle derailleur and two weeks of labor for it, and spent another six months sourcing the oscillator crystal and the capacitors and the solder and the patience to make it run. The cabinet had left a faint grid of rust marks on the bottom of the case, like a scar it had earned.

She pulled the stool out from under the table and sat down.

The logbook was already open to tonight's page. She uncapped the pen, a mechanical pencil, 0.5mm, the last lead stick in a tube she'd been rationing for eight months, and read back.

Three pages.

She read them the way she always read them at the end of a session: not looking for something she'd missed, but checking her own handwriting against her memory of the night, making sure the notation was clean. It was a habit from before. In the old world, signal logs had to be legible to someone other than the person who wrote them. She'd kept the habit because it was the only thing that made the logs feel like they were for something beyond herself.

*2200 local. 7.200 MHz. Noise floor elevated. No carriers. S1 background, no modulation. Logged.*

*2215. 9.410 MHz. Faint heterodyne, possibly propagation artifact. No voice, no CW. Duration approx. 4 sec. Not repeated. Logged.*

*2230. 6.070 MHz. Dead. 5.900 MHz. Dead. 5.800 MHz. Dead.*

The entries continued down the page in her private shorthand, the frequencies in descending order as she'd swept the bands, the signal strengths noted with the S-meter notation she'd used since she was nineteen years old and her father had shown her how to use his old Kenwood in the garage. S1. S1. S0. S1. The occasional S2 that turned out to be atmospheric noise or the ghost of a carrier from somewhere so distant it had lost all meaning by the time it reached her. Nothing that resolved into voice. Nothing that carried information. Nothing that suggested, even faintly, that someone else was out there doing what she was doing, sitting in a small room in the dark, pointing an antenna at the sky, waiting.

She turned back one more page. Two nights ago.

The same.

She turned back another. Three nights ago.

The same.

She had 2,547 of these pages. She knew the number because she had numbered them, because numbering was a way of making the accumulation feel like something other than what it was. The first hundred pages she had filled with real hope, the kind of hope that is almost indistinguishable from certainty, the kind that makes you check the same frequency twice because you're sure you heard something and it turned out to be your own pulse in your ears. The next three hundred she had filled with a more careful hope, the kind that knows it might be wrong but hasn't yet accepted it. Somewhere around page eight hundred she had stopped thinking of herself as listening for something and started thinking of herself as maintaining a record. A record of silence. A record of the fact that on this night, at this frequency, at this hour, there was nothing. Which was, she had told herself, still information. Absence was data. The silence was a finding.

She had believed that for a long time.

She turned back to tonight's page and wrote the final entry.

*2347 local. Full sweep complete. 7, 21 MHz, primary bands. No carriers. No voice. No CW. No modulation of any kind. Conditions: noise floor moderate, no unusual solar activity noted. Visibility clear. Wind NW, approx. 15 kph. Receiver functional. Calibration drift +0.4 kHz at current temp, compensated.*

She paused, pencil still touching the paper.

She wrote: *Night 2,547.*

Then she capped the pencil and closed the book.

The receiver was still running. She could hear it, not the signal, there was no signal, there was never a signal, but the receiver itself, the faint electrical whisper of a circuit doing its job in an empty room. The squelch was open and the speaker was live and what came out of it was the sound the universe made when no one was transmitting: a soft, continuous hiss, textured with tiny pops and crackles, the ionosphere shedding its own noise into the dark. It was not an unpleasant sound. She had slept to it, in the early years, before she'd learned to sleep without it.

She put her hand on the receiver.

The case was cool under her palm. The Grundig had a solidity to it that most salvaged electronics had lost, a pre-Cascade weight, the density of components built when someone still believed the thing would be used for decades. She could feel the faint vibration of the speaker through the plastic. The hiss. The nothing.

She sat with her hand there for a moment.

She thought about Dani, which she tried not to do at this hour because this hour was already its own kind of difficult. She thought about the crossed-out lines in the logbook from the first year. *Nothing I could have done.* She thought about the oscillator crystal that was not quite the right cut, the 10.000 MHz where 11.0592 should have been, close enough to work if you adjusted around it. She thought about close enough as a philosophy and what it cost.

The receiver hissed.

She switched it off.

The silence that followed was a different kind of silence, not the ionosphere's silence, which was full of its own small noise, but the silence of a circuit gone dead, a thing that had been attending and was now simply absent. It was a heavier silence. She had never gotten used to it.

She sat in it for a moment anyway.

Then she picked up the logbook, tucked it under her arm, and went to bed.

She was almost asleep when she heard it.

Not a signal. She knew what signals sounded like, the crisp carrier tone, the sudden lift in the noise floor, the way a voice or a code burst would cut through static with the unmistakable quality of intention. This was not that. This was something she had not switched the receiver back on to hear, because she had not switched the receiver back on. The room was dark and the circuit was dead and what she had heard was nothing.

Except.

She lay still. Her eyes were open. The ceiling was invisible above her, no moon tonight, and she kept the blackout shutters latched because light was an invitation she couldn't afford. The farmhouse settled around her, the slow tick of cooling timber, the loose aluminum flashing on the north gable that rattled when the wind found it. Northwest wind tonight. She had noted it in the log.

The sound she had heard, or had not heard, had been on 7.850 MHz.

She knew this the way she knew things in the interval between waking and sleep, without being able to explain the knowing. She had swept through 7.850 during the last pass and written S1, background, no modulation, the same as every band in the sweep. But something had snagged at the edge of her attention and she had moved on, because she always moved on, because after 2,547 nights you did not stop at every slight irregularity in the noise floor or you would never finish a sweep at all.

She stared at the ceiling.

It was probably ionospheric. A pocket of disturbed F-layer, a skip anomaly, a faint carrier from a transmitter so distant its modulation had been stripped away by the time it reached her antenna and what remained was just the ghost of a carrier, a slight asymmetry in the noise that her pattern-hungry brain had filed as almost something.

The brain did this. She knew it did this. She had documented it doing this, pages in the logbook from the first year marked with small notations: *probable auditory artifact, not repeated, disregard.* The brain was a signal-detection machine and it was poorly calibrated for silence. It found patterns in noise because finding patterns in noise was what kept early humans alive and it did not care that there were no more early humans and the noise was just the ionosphere shedding electrons into the dark.

She turned onto her side.

The wind moved the flashing on the north gable.

She turned onto her back.

The thing about 7.850 was that it was not a frequency she expected anything on. The religious broadcasters had mostly clustered around 9.4 and 11.7 in the years after the Cascade, when there had still been religious broadcasters, she'd logged a Spanish-language station out of somewhere in the southwest running until night 340, and a shortlived English-language outfit that had broadcast the same three recorded sermons on a loop until its generator apparently gave out around night 180. The utility traffic that still occasionally surfaced came mostly from the lower end of the HF spectrum, 3 to 5 MHz, weak and drifting. 7.850 was quiet. Had always been quiet. Was probably quiet now.

She got up.

She did not turn on a light. She knew the farmhouse by feel, the four steps to the workroom door, the slight give in the third floorboard, the height of the workbench. She sat down in the dark and found the receiver by its shape and turned it on.

The circuit woke with its usual reluctance, the audio coming up thin and hissy before the components warmed, the S-meter needle swinging up and settling. She could not see the needle. She put her fingertip lightly against the face of the dial and felt it, the slight vibration of the needle resting at S1, the baseline, the nothing.

She tuned to 7.850.

Static. The particular texture of the 40-meter band at this hour, a medium hiss with occasional low pops, the ionosphere doing what it always did. She sat with it. She did not reach for the logbook because she had not heard anything and she was not going to log the absence of a signal she had imagined.

She sat for three minutes. Maybe four. The receiver hissed. The flashing on the north gable ticked once in the wind and went quiet.

And there it was.

Not a carrier. Not a voice. Just a faint asymmetry in the texture of the noise, a slight thickening, a density that was almost rhythmic, that lasted perhaps two seconds and then dissolved back into the hiss so completely she could not have said where it had ended. It was the difference between white noise and noise that was very slightly not white. It was the kind of thing you could convince yourself you had not heard.

She sat very still.

Her hand was on the tuning knob but she did not move it. She breathed through her nose, slowly, the way she had learned to breathe when she was listening for something at the edge of audibility, the way her father had taught her, *don't hold your breath, you'll hear your pulse and your pulse will lie to you.*

The static hissed.

Nothing.

Nothing.

The slight thickening again, two seconds, maybe three, a texture in the noise that was almost a pulse, almost a pattern, almost nothing at all.

She took her hand off the tuning knob. She put both hands flat on the workbench.

It was ionospheric. It was a propagation artifact, a skip anomaly, a faint carrier from somewhere so far away that its structure had been entirely stripped by distance and what remained was only the faintest imprint of having once been structured, the way a pressed flower still held the ghost of its original shape. It was her own pattern-hungry brain doing what it always did. It was nothing.

She sat with it for another two minutes. The asymmetry came again, twice, she thought, though the second time she was less sure, and then the band shifted slightly as the ionosphere adjusted to whatever the ionosphere adjusted to at this hour, and the noise flattened back to its ordinary texture, and 7.850 was just 7.850 again, dead and featureless.

She turned the receiver off.

She did not open the logbook. There was nothing to log. She had heard ionospheric noise with a slight irregularity that her brain had briefly mistaken for structure, and she had gotten out of bed to confirm that she had been mistaken, and she had confirmed it, and now she was going back to bed.

She stood up from the workbench.

In the dark, the receiver sat where she had left it, the Grundig's solid pre-Cascade weight, its dial face invisible, its speaker silent. She could not see the S-meter needle. She knew it was resting at zero, or just off zero, the baseline position, the nothing position, the position the needle always returned to when the circuit was dead and there was no signal and there had never been a signal and the world was as quiet as it had been for seven years.

She went back to bed.

She lay in the dark and listened to the farmhouse settle and the aluminum flashing tick in the northwest wind and the particular quality of silence that followed a circuit going dead, and she told herself, with the flat certainty of someone who has learned not to hope at this hour, that she had heard nothing.

The needle, in the dark workroom, rested just off zero.

It trembled once, the faint mechanical sympathy of a circuit not quite fully discharged, the last ghost of current moving through a coil, and then it was still.

research_gaps: Confirm Grundig Satellit 750 survival likelihood in a steel filing cabinet during a solar superstorm EMP-adjacent event — clarify whether the Cascade is CME-induced geomagnetic storm or nuclear EMP, as the physics differ significantly for shielding
Verify 7.850 MHz is plausible for the described propagation behavior at the described hour and season — 40-meter band skip characteristics at night
Lead-acid battery trickle-charge behavior from a small solar panel over seven years — confirm whether this is realistic without replacement cells

result.research_facts:
- **Shortwave bands**: Shortwave radio uses the high-frequency spectrum roughly from 2 to 30 MHz, and signals can travel long distances by reflecting off the ionosphere, which is why distant stations can sometimes be heard as sudden fade-ins, bursts of heterodyne tone, or layered voices in static.[9][10] In a post-Cascade setting, a receiver left scanning the bands would realistically catch intermittent utility traffic, religious broadcasters, and whatever surviving transmitters still had power.[3][5]

- **Listening conditions**: Shortwave reception changes with time of day, season, and solar/ionospheric conditions, so the same frequency can be clear one night and dead the next.[10] That makes careful logging believable: operators typically note frequency, time, signal strength, and whether the voice is intelligible, drifting, or buried under noise.[4][10]

- **Receiver behavior**: A salvaged shortwave set would be full of telltale problems after years of neglect: scratchy tuning, drifting calibration, oxidized contacts, weak audio, and batteries or improvised power supplies that sag under load.[4][9] Even when functioning, the audio would usually be narrow, hissy, and prone to fading in and out rather than clean and continuous.[5][9]

- **Static and interference**: Solar and atmospheric disturbances can raise the noise floor and make bands sound like continuous hiss with occasional pops, whistles, and warbling carriers.[9][10] In a world where much electrical infrastructure is gone, local interference would be less from cities and more from whatever generators, scavenged inverters, battery chargers, or makeshift electronics still exist nearby.

- **Fortified farmhouse practicals**: A farmstead surviving after infrastructure collapse would plausibly rely on thick, insulating walls, shuttered openings, improvised barriers, and a strict separation between living space, storage, and workshop areas. The most useful atmosphere is utilitarian: seed tins, hand tools, patched tarps, water barrels, nail-scarred boards, and fuel or battery stores kept under lock because everything portable has value.

- **Water and food storage**: In a broken suburban edge environment, preserved food would matter more than fresh variety: dried beans, grain, canned goods, root crops, salt, vinegar, and rendered fats are all realistic survival staples. Water would likely be collected from roofs or wells and stored in covered containers to reduce contamination, algae, and evaporation.

- **Repair economy**: Trading repaired equipment for food fits a collapse economy because small reliable tools become more valuable than currency. Items with lasting worth would include hand-cranked lamps, radios, bicycle parts, knives, needles, batteries, wire, solder, ceramic insulators, and pump components.

- **Dead suburb details**: A “dead suburb” would still be full of low, repetitive domestic infrastructure—driveways, fences, mailboxes, cul-de-sacs, detached garages, and weed-choked lawns—now stripped, cracked, or collapsed. Quiet here would feel physical because without traffic, HVAC hum, and neighborhood power noise, ordinary sounds like wind in gutters, loose siding, and distant animals become prominent.

- **Seven years after collapse**: After several years without regular industrial supply chains, asphalt would crack, roofs would leak, and many metal fixtures would rust while glass, plastics, and ceramics lingered as scattered debris. Roads would remain usable in patches but would be broken by frost heave, root growth, sinkholes, and abandoned vehicles slowly being cannibalized for parts.

- **Shortwave terminology**: A radio operator in Mara’s place would naturally think in terms like frequency, band, carrier, drift, skip, noise floor, S-meter, modulation, and QRM for interference.[9][10] If she hears a repeating encrypted signal, the most plausible immediate reaction is to measure its interval and note whether it sits on a fixed carrier or rides with slight wobble.

sub_chapter_briefs.title: Dani's Watch

sub_chapter_briefs.title: 2,547 Nights of Nothing
sub_chapter_briefs.beat: Mara returns to the radio room for her final scan of the night; she reads back through three pages of her logbook — all silence, all notation, all the same — and we understand that she has been listening for something she no longer believes exists; she writes the night's final entry, closes the book, and sits for a long moment with her hand on the receiver before switching it off.

sub_chapter_briefs.title: Static
sub_chapter_briefs.beat: In the last minutes before sleep, Mara hears something — not a signal, not yet, just a faint asymmetry in the static on 7.850 MHz, a texture that is almost pattern; she tells herself it is ionospheric noise, writes nothing in the logbook, and goes to bed; the final image is the receiver's needle resting just off zero in the dark, trembling.
